# The Physics of Connection

> Seven laws, nine principles — discovered on the improv stage, applicable everywhere. A knowledge graph for the art of human connection.

The Physics of Connection applies improv principles to everyday human challenges: overthinking, awkwardness, team dynamics, listening, assertiveness, public speaking, and more. The material is grounded in roughly sixty years of improv practice across five traditions (Johnstone, Spolin, Close/Halpern, UCB, Annoyance/TJ & Dave), and cites its primary sources.

This file is generated from the site's content and its sitemap, so it lists every page rather than a selection. Sections run from the entry points to the primitives: guides first, then the laws and concepts they rest on, then the lessons and paths that teach them. Within a section, guides are ordered by the search demand they answer and concepts by how many other concepts depend on them.

## Guides (78)

- [Conversation Starters: 192 That Survive the Second Exchange](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/conversation-starters): A starter only buys you one exchange. What you do with the second decides the rest. 192 sorted by the room you are in, and why the clever ones die fastest. For: you open with something fine and the conversation is dead within thirty seconds.
- [10 Public Speaking Tips for the Parts You Cannot Rehearse](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/public-speaking-tips): Most public speaking tips cover the prepared talk. What actually goes wrong is everything you could not rehearse — and that is what improv trains. For: you are fine until somebody asks a question you did not prepare for.
- [Would You Rather Questions: 164 That Split the Room](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/would-you-rather-questions): A would you rather only works if the room genuinely divides. The choice is never the point — the defence is, and most lists get that exactly backwards. For: you ask a would you rather and everybody says it depends and the game dies.
- [Team Building Activities That Actually Change Teams](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/team-building-activities): Most team building is theater — fun in the moment, zero behavioral change on Monday. Here's what improv reveals about activities that actually work.
- [189 Icebreaker Questions to Get to Know Someone](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/questions-to-get-to-know-someone): The icebreaker questions that work are the unglamorous ones: everybody already has the answer, three words is a complete turn, and nobody is being scored. For: you meet someone you might like and the conversation stays on weather and jobs.
- [Deep Questions to Ask: 153 That Get an Honest Answer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/deep-questions-to-ask): Most deep questions ask for a conclusion, so they get a performance. These ask for an experience — plus what has to be true before any of them work at all. For: you ask something real and get an answer that sounds like a CV.
- [Questions for Couples: 124 That Update What You Know](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/questions-for-couples): With a partner the problem is never trust. It is that you stopped updating — you answer on their behalf without checking, and you have been wrong for a while. For: you know each other completely and have not learned anything new in about two years.
- [Networking Tips That Work If You Hate Networking](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/networking-tips): Networking feels bad because it is framed as extraction, and everyone can tell. The fix is not a better opener — it is arriving with something to offer. For: you go to the event, collect three business cards, and feel slightly grubby afterwards.
- [Most Likely To Questions: 182 That Land as a Compliment](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/most-likely-to-questions): The only question game where the answer is about somebody else in the room — which makes it recognition when it works and a roast when it does not. For: the game was going well and then somebody got named for something that was not funny.
- [21 Questions Game: How to Play, and 181 to Ask](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/21-questions-game): The number is the mechanism. A fixed count removes the polite exit at question six and guarantees an ending, which is the only reason this gets anywhere real. For: the conversation is fine and stops at the first polite opportunity every time.
- [Questions to Ask Friends: 152 That Go Somewhere](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/questions-to-ask-friends): Most question lists optimise for an interesting answer. These are sorted by what happens after it, and by the one thing that decides whether a question lands. For: you want to talk about something other than work and neither of you knows how to start.
- [This or That Questions: 300 for Warming Up Any Room](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/this-or-that-questions): The cheapest question format there is — one word, nothing to prepare. Which makes it the right tool for a cold room and the wrong one for a warm one. For: the room is cold and every question you ask lands with a thud.
- [How to Read Body Language: What Improv Reveals](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-read-body-language): Body language isn't a code to decode — it's a conversation to join. Improv performers read bodies in real time under pressure. Here's what they've learned.
- [Questions to Ask a Girl: Why the List Is Not the Problem](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/questions-to-ask-a-girl): The gendering is the mistake. Nothing about getting to know somebody changes by who they are — what changes it is whether you are exchanging or extracting. For: you like somebody and every question you can think of sounds like an interview.
- [Party Games: 40 That Need Nothing but People](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/party-games): Most party game lists are shopping lists. These need no equipment, no setup and no explaining — and they survive somebody joining halfway through. For: the party has gone quiet and everything you can think of requires props nobody has.
- [How to Be a Better Leader: Coach Without Taking Over](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-a-better-manager): Your job is not to have the best ideas — it is to make other people's work land. Improv trains the authority a group concedes, not the kind a title grants. For: the team defers to you and you cannot tell whether they agree.
- [36 Questions to Fall in Love: The List and the Mechanism](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/36-questions-to-fall-in-love): The full set from Aron's 1997 study, plus what the lists leave out: what the procedure was built to do, and why the escalation does the work. For: you have heard the questions make strangers fall in love and want to know whether that is true.
- [Questions to Ask in an Interview, and at the End of One](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/questions-to-ask-in-an-interview): Your questions are the one move that levels the status gap. What to ask an interviewer when they turn it over to you, and the ones that cost you the offer. For: you get to the end of the interview and the only question you can think of is about the next steps.
- [Funny Questions to Ask: 100 That Make the Answer Funny](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/funny-questions-to-ask): A funny question is not one with a joke in it — that joke is spent before anyone answers. These make the other person funny, which is the only kind that runs. For: you ask the funny question, everyone laughs at the question, and then nobody has anything to say.
- [Icebreaker Questions for Work: 123 People Will Answer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/icebreaker-questions-for-work): Work icebreakers fail for a structural reason, not a creative one — you are asking for disclosure in a room with a power gap. These are built for that. For: you have to open a meeting and every icebreaker you can think of makes people wince.
- [Fun Questions to Ask Friends: 116 Worth Actually Answering](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/fun-questions-to-ask-friends): Fun is not the same as funny, and it is not shallow. It comes down to whether a question asks you to invent something or just to look something up. For: you want the conversation to be fun and every list you find is either party trivia or therapy.
- [Active Listening Skills: Why You're Doing It Wrong](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/active-listening): Most active listening advice teaches you to perform attention while composing a reply. Here's the mechanism that makes fake listening impossible. For: you stop receiving because you are composing your reply.
- [Virtual Team Building Activities That Work on a Call](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/virtual-team-building-activities): Most virtual team building is an in-person activity ported onto video, where every constraint that made it work has gone. These are built for the call itself. For: you run the activity that worked in the office and on video it dies.
- [How to Make Friends as an Adult: The Ensemble Problem](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-make-friends-as-an-adult): Adults don't lose the skill of making friends. They lose the conditions it needs — repeated contact and shared low-stakes activity. Both can be rebuilt. For: you get on with people fine and none of it turns into friendship.
- [How to Stop Overthinking and Get Out of Your Head](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-stop-overthinking): Overthinking is not a thinking problem, it is a bandwidth problem — which is why you cannot think your way out of your head. What works instead. For: you freeze because your attention collapses into planning.
- [How to Be More Confident (Without Faking It)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-more-confident): Confidence isn't a feeling you summon — it's a byproduct of commitment. Full commitment to any choice reads as confidence. Half-commitment reads as doubt.
- [Psychological Safety: The Physics of Trust](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/psychological-safety): Psychological safety isn't about being nice. It's about specific behaviors that make risk feel safe. Here's what improv ensembles learned about trust.
- [Team Building Questions That Actually Build Trust](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/team-building-questions): Most team building questions are trivially safe or performatively deep. Neither builds trust. Here's the improv principle that does — and 20 questions.
- [How to Be Funny (It's Not What You Think)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-funny): Funny isn't a skill you add on top. It's what happens when two people are honest and specific together. Here's what 50 years of improv reveals about humor. For: trying to be clever is making the moment feel forced.
- [Social Awkwardness Is an Attention Problem, Not a Trait](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-less-awkward): Social awkwardness is not a personality trait. It is what happens when attention turns inward at the moment it needed to be outward — and that is trainable. For: self-monitoring is louder than connection.
- [Team Dynamics: The Invisible Architecture of a Group](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/team-dynamics): Team dynamics are not personality clashes. They are status transactions, signalling and coherence — and improv ensembles decoded them decades ago.
- [How to Stop Caring What People Think: The Performer's Secret](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-stop-caring-what-people-think): The fear of judgment isn't weakness — it's a misfire of your social-threat system. Improv performers face it nightly and know how to disarm it.
- [How to Keep a Conversation Going Without More Topics](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-keep-a-conversation-going): Conversations don't die from a shortage of topics. They die from redirects. Improv shows why, and the three moves that keep an exchange alive.
- [Theatre Games: What They Are and How to Run Them](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/theatre-games): Theatre games were invented to teach non-actors, not to get laughs. Here's where they came from, how they differ from improv games, and how to run them. For: you need structured drama exercises that build skills rather than just fill time.
- [How to Be Vulnerable (Without Getting Destroyed)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-vulnerable): Vulnerability isn't emotional exhibition — it's the willingness to make an offer that could be rejected. The secret is building the container first.
- [How to Be a Good Friend: The Support Most People Miss](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-a-good-friend): Most bad friending is well-intentioned blocking — solving, redirecting, reassuring. Improv names each one, and what to do instead of all of them. For: you care about them and they have stopped telling you things.
- [How to Make Small Talk: The Improv Method](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-make-small-talk): Small talk fails when you treat it as performance. Improv reveals it's actually a collaboration — and the skills that make it work are learnable.
- [How to Stop People Pleasing: The Authentic Response](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-stop-people-pleasing): People pleasing is blocking in disguise: refusing your own offers to protect someone else's comfort. Improv reveals the mechanism — and the way out.
- [Improv Prompts: 140 Scene Starters for Class or Stage](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/improv-prompts): 140 prompts you can use tonight — relationships, first lines, locations, classroom sets — plus how to run a round with a full class. For: you need something to start a scene with and everything you think of is either boring or too clever.
- [The Framing Effect: The Skill That Looks Like a Bias](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/framing-effect): The framing effect is usually taught as a bias to defend against. It's also a skill — one improv performers have trained for sixty years.
- [How to Be a Good Listener (Not the Kind You Think)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-a-good-listener): Most listening advice tells you to nod and paraphrase. Real listening — the kind improv performers stake their careers on — works completely differently.
- [How to Be More Creative: Stop Trying to Be Original](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-more-creative): Creativity isn't originality — it's the willingness to follow the obvious. The more obvious you are, the more original you appear. Here's the science.
- [How to Be More Charismatic: The Presence Framework](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-more-charismatic): Charisma isn't a trait — it's a specific combination of presence, commitment, and status fluency. Improv performers train all three. Here's how.
- [How to Deal with Rejection: Failing Forward](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-deal-with-rejection): Rejection hurts because your brain treats social exclusion like physical pain. Improv performers face it nightly and have a system for metabolizing it.
- [Glossophobia: The Fear of Public Speaking, Reframed](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/fear-of-public-speaking): Glossophobia is the fear of public speaking. What it is, when it is ordinary nerves and when it is not, and what performers do instead of removing it.
- [How to Be More Assertive: The Status Secret from Improv](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-more-assertive): Assertiveness isn't aggression — it's a physical and vocal pattern improv calls 'status.' It's learnable, and doesn't require changing who you are.
- [How to Have Difficult Conversations: The Improv Approach](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-have-difficult-conversations): Difficult conversations fail when people plan scripts and defend positions. Improv teaches another way: listen first, respond to what's real.
- [Active Listening Exercises That Actually Train It](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/active-listening-exercises): Most listening exercises rehearse looking attentive. These eleven make composing your reply structurally impossible — seven for pairs, four for a group. For: you know you should listen better and practising it never seems to change anything.
- [How to Be More Articulate: It Is Not About Vocabulary](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-more-articulate): You can be intelligent and inarticulate — they run on different constraints. Articulate people are not thinking faster, they have fewer processes running. For: you know what you mean and it comes out as three false starts and a shrug.
- [Anne Bogart Viewpoints: The Nine Channels](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/viewpoints): Bogart and Landau turned Overlie's six Viewpoints into nine channels of attention. What each one is, how they are trained, and where the method fails.
- [People Skills Are a System, Not a Personality Trait](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/people-skills): Most people-skills advice is a parts catalogue — eye contact, I-statements, paraphrasing. It is a real-time system, and the mechanics are learnable.
- [Yes And Improv: The Rule Everyone Gets Wrong](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/yes-and-improv): Yes and is improv's most quoted rule and its most misunderstood. What it actually means, where it came from, and where it stops working at work.
- [Del Close: The Ideas That Still Run Improv](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/del-close): Del Close invented the Harold and taught two generations of Chicago improvisers. What he actually believed, what holds up, and what the mythology hides.
- [How to Be Present: The Bandwidth Trick That Actually Works](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-present): Presence isn't a spiritual practice — it's a bandwidth allocation problem. Your brain has finite processing capacity, and internal chatter hogs it.
- [Stage Fright Is Not Your Enemy](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/stage-fright): Stage fright and peak performance have identical physiology. The difference is a single cognitive reframe. Here's the practice that turns fear into fuel. For: fear is making you hesitate instead of making the first move.
- [5-Minute Team Building Activities That Actually Work](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/5-minute-team-building): You don't need an escape room. Twenty improv exercises that shift how a group interacts, grouped by what is actually wrong with the room.
- [Emotional Safety: What It Is and How It Gets Built](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/emotional-safety): Emotional safety is the confidence that showing what you feel will not be used against you. It is built by repetition, not by announcement — here is how.
- [How to Deal with Conflict: The Acceptance Paradox](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-deal-with-conflict): Most conflict advice says 'communicate better' without explaining the mechanism. Conflict escalates when people block each other's reality. Here's the fix.
- [How to Let Go of Control: What Improv Teaches](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-let-go-of-control): Control feels safe but kills connection. Improv performers surrender it every night — and the results beat anything they could have planned.
- [Viola Spolin: The Woman Who Invented Theater Games](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/viola-spolin): Spolin built improv's teaching method before improv existed as a form — and she built it in social work, not theatre. What she actually invented, and why.
- [Confidence Building Exercises That Aren't Affirmations](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/confidence-building-exercises): Confidence is not a feeling you generate before acting — it is what accumulates after acting anyway. Seven exercises for pairs, six you can do alone. For: you keep waiting to feel ready and the moment keeps passing.
- [How to Overcome Fear of Failure: The Improv Reframe](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-overcome-fear-of-failure): Fear of failure is really fear of irreversibility — the belief a wrong move is permanent. Improv's insight: everything is an offer to build on.
- [Trust Building Exercises That Aren't Trust Falls](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/trust-building-exercises): Trust is not built by dramatic gestures but by small repeated exchanges. Seven exercises that rehearse them — for a team, or for two people. For: the team is polite but nobody says the real thing.
- [How to Be Witty: The Improv Secret to Quick, Sharp Responses](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-be-witty): Witty people aren't faster thinkers — they're less filtered ones. Improv training reveals why your best responses come when you stop trying to be clever.
- [How to Stop Overthinking in a Relationship](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-stop-overthinking-in-a-relationship): Relationship overthinking has a specific mechanism — social-threat bandwidth hijacking. The fix requires both trust and presence, together.
- [Improv Games for Kids: What Works at Each Age](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/improv-games-for-kids): Most improv games fail with children because they were built for people who volunteered. Which games work at which age, and how to run them with thirty. For: you have thirty children, forty minutes, and the last game you tried turned into shouting.
- [How to Read the Room: The Skill Performers Train](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-read-the-room): Reading a room means working out what a group feels and is ready for, not what it says. It is not intuition but a set of attention skills, and they train.
- [The Rules of Improv (And Why Half of Them Are Wrong)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/rules-of-improv): Every improv class teaches the same rules. But the five major traditions disagree on what they are. Here's what matters, what's myth, and what works.
- [Types of Listening: The Three Modes That Matter](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/types-of-listening): Three attention modes — broadcast, evaluative, receptive — the seven conventional types mapped onto them, and when each one helps or kills a conversation.
- [How to Give Feedback That Actually Changes Behavior](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-give-feedback): Most feedback describes problems without creating conditions for change. Design experiences where the right behavior emerges naturally, then name it.
- [How to Think on Your Feet When You Are Put on the Spot](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-think-on-your-feet): Thinking on your feet is not fast thinking. It is starting to speak before you have the whole answer, and the difference is trainable. For: somebody asks what you think, everybody turns, and your mind produces nothing.
- [Collaboration Skills: What Improv Ensembles Know](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/collaboration-skills): Real collaboration isn't brainstorming or consensus — it's building on each other's ideas in real time. Improv ensembles train this skill every night.
- [What Is Improv? How Unscripted Theatre Works](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/what-is-improv): Improv is unscripted theatre built in real time from offers. What happens on stage, short form versus long form, where it came from, and how to start. For: you need a clear model of what improv actually is and how scenes stay alive.
- [How to Get Better at Improv: A Practitioner's Guide](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-to-get-better-at-improv): Getting better at improv isn't about doing more shows. It's about diagnosing what's actually breaking and practicing the specific skill that fixes it.
- [Improv Team Building: What Actually Transfers to Work](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/improv-team-building): The claim is oversold and the useful part is real. What improv training genuinely changes about a team, what it does not, and why the away-day fails. For: somebody has suggested booking an improv workshop and you cannot tell whether it is worth the afternoon.
- [Improv Warm-Up Games: The Order Matters More Than the Game](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/improv-warm-up-games): A warm-up is a sequence, not a game you pick at random. Three stages that move a room from arrival to playing, with the games that do each job. For: you have a room of people who have just arrived from their day and twenty minutes to make them playable.
- [Improv Theory: The Five Traditions That Shaped It](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/improv-theory): Johnstone, Spolin, Close, UCB, and Annoyance built improv on different foundations. Here's where they agree, where they clash, and why it matters.
- [2 Person Improv Games: What Two People Can Actually Do](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/2-person-improv-games): Most improv games quietly assume a circle of eight. These do not. What a pair can train alone, what they cannot, and how to run a session. For: you have one person to practise with and every game you find needs a room full of people.

## Laws — the underlying physics (7)

- [Shared Reality Is Fragile](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/shared-reality-fragility): The shared reality of an improv scene — that you're in a freezer, that you're husband and wife — isn't physically real. There are no walls, no costumes.
- [Cognitive Bandwidth](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/cognitive-bandwidth): Attention is limited. Action consumes capacity. Simultaneous optimization is impossible.
- [Meaning Is Relational](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/meaning-is-relational): Meaning is completed in reception, not in intention. What an offer means is settled by what the other person does with it, which is why solo effort fails.
- [Continuous Signaling](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/continuous-signaling): You signal continuously. You are always communicating, whether you intend to or not.
- [Irreversibility (Path Dependence)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/irreversibility): Time advances irreversibly. Once a signal is sent, it becomes part of the shared history. You cannot edit, undo, or retract.
- [Interdependence](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/interdependence): You cannot build a shared reality alone. No one performer has the bandwidth or the perspective, and the shortfall is structural rather than a lack of skill.
- [Belief as Architecture](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/belief-as-architecture): People defend their belief systems by default — not as a preference, but as architecture.

## Principles — behavioural guidelines (9)

- [Be Present](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-present): Let external reality take priority over internal computation. Receive what is happening now; respond before it moves on.
- [Be Brave](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-brave): Act before you're ready. The scene needs offers more than it needs perfect offers. Every other principle assumes data is already flowing.
- [Be Honest](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-honest): Signal the shared reality as it currently exists, clearly and without distortion.
- [Be Changeable](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-changeable): Let your partner's offers transform your state — your plans, your emotions, your character, your history.
- [Be Supportive](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-supportive): Make your partner's choices look brilliant. Optimize for the ensemble, not for yourself.
- [Be Simple](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-simple): Prefer simple, obvious actions — they create space for depth and are gifts your partner can immediately use. The most counterintuitive principle.
- [Be Positive](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-positive): Accept the current state and extend it forward, rather than resisting or undoing it. "Positive" doesn't mean happy.
- [Be Thankful](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/be-thankful): Treat every outcome as usable information and postpone evaluation. This sounds nice but it's a tactical maneuver.
- [Framing as Angle of Approach](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/principles/framing-as-angle-of-approach): The content of an idea and the angle at which it arrives are not the same thing.

## Insights (5)

- [Reality Construction](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/reality-construction): Reality Construction is the central reframe: improv isn't about comedy. Comedy is a byproduct.
- [Model of Their Model](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/model-of-their-model): You cannot see into another person's mind. You only ever have your model of their model — a second-order representation.
- [Performance State](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/performance-state): The state a performer works from: nervous arousal and relaxed openness at the same time. Why the sensation of dread and of readiness are identical.
- [Beyond the Stage](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/beyond-the-stage): The principles of improv are not theater techniques. They are the operating requirements for human connection.
- [Finding Your Voice](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/finding-your-voice): Finding Your Voice is the emergence over years of practice of a recognizable artistic identity — a characteristic set of choices, instincts, interests.

## Failure modes and patterns (21)

- [Heightening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/heightening): Heightening is the pattern of escalating the game of the scene — repeating the core behavioral pattern while raising the stakes, expanding the context.
- [Discovery](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/discovery): Discovery is the moment when both players recognize what the scene is about — when the game, the pattern.
- [Internal Computation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/internal-computation): Internal Computation is the shadow of Be Present. Internal computation is the act of retreating into your own head — planning, rehearsing, evaluating.
- [Hesitation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/hesitation): Hesitation is the shadow of Be Brave. Hesitation is the failure to act at a decision point — not just at the threshold of a scene.
- [Performing Cleverness](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/performing-cleverness): Performing Cleverness is the shadow of Be Honest. Performing cleverness is the substitution of authentic signal with a display of wit.
- [Blocking](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/blocking): Blocking is the general term for any behavior that refuses, deflects, or undermines the offers in a scene.
- [Callback](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/callback): Callback is the pattern of referencing an earlier established detail — a name, an object, a line, a gesture — later in the scene or show.
- [Judgment (Mid-Scene Evaluation)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/judgment): Judgment (Mid-Scene Evaluation) is the shadow of Be Thankful. Judgment is the act of evaluating a move — yours or your partner's.
- [Negation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/negation): Negation is the shadow of Be Positive. Negation is specifically the contradiction of established reality.
- [Bulldozing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/bulldozing): Bulldozing is the shadow of Be Supportive. Bulldozing is moving through a scene with no attention to your partner's offers, pushing only your own ideas.
- [Steering](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/steering): Steering is the shadow of Be Changeable — accepting your partner's offers on the surface while redirecting the scene where you had already decided to go.
- [Systemic Collapse Modes](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/systemic-collapse-modes): Systemic Collapse Modes are the warning lights. How shared reality falls apart. Three modes of collapse: Response latency increases.
- [Recovery: Decay](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/decay-recovery): Decay is how to recover when the scene has gone thin — when established facts have faded, nothing accumulates, and the shared reality feels weightless.
- [Recovery: Fracture](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/fracture-recovery): Fracture is how to recover when two players are in different scenes — the shared state has split and neither can tell why it feels off.
- [Overcomplication](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/overcomplication): Overcomplication is the shadow of Be Simple. Overcomplication is flooding the shared channel with more data than it can carry.
- [Systemic Health Indicators](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/systemic-health-indicators): Systemic Health Indicators are the gauges on the dashboard. How you know the scene is working while you're inside it. Judge the process, not the product.
- [Recovery: Latency](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/latency-recovery): Latency is how to recover when the scene has developed response lag — when one or both players are behind the moment.
- [Wimping](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/wimping): Wimping is accepting an offer and adding nothing to it. Johnstone's term for the politest way to stop a scene.
- [The Blocking Taxonomy](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/blocking-taxonomy): Johnstone's central observation about refusal is that almost nobody does it out loud.
- [Rigid Core, Malleable Edge](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/rigid-core-malleable-edge): Beliefs are not defended uniformly. Every belief system has a core — the identity-anchored commitments that produce rejection on contact — and an edge.
- [Diagnosing Scene Failure](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/how-it-works/diagnosis/diagnosing-scene-failure): Diagnosing Scene Failure is a procedure for turning "that scene didn't work" into something you can practise.

## Vocabulary — improv terms defined (31)

- [Offers](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/offers): An offer is anything that advances the scene — any word, gesture, expression, movement, or silence that adds to the shared reality.
- [Ensemble](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/ensemble): Ensemble is the group of performers operating as a single creative unit. Not a collection of individuals taking turns.
- [Game of the Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/game-of-the-scene): Game of the Scene is the repeatable, heightenable pattern that gives a scene structure and momentum — the thing the scene is "about" behaviorally.
- [Relationship](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/relationship): Relationship is the connection between characters in a scene — who they are to each other, what they feel about each other.
- [Group Mind](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/group-mind): Group Mind is the emergent phenomenon where an ensemble operates as if it shares a single creative intelligence — making complementary choices.
- [Status](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/status): Status is the relative social position a character occupies in a scene, expressed through behavior rather than title or rank.
- [Signal](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/signal): A signal is any information transmitted from one participant to another, whether intentional or not.
- [Trust](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/trust): Trust is the foundation that makes every other principle safe to practice. Without trust, bravery is recklessness, honesty is exposure.
- [Character](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/character): Character is a distinct identity inhabited by the performer — with its own way of seeing the world, its own desires, its own physical life.
- [Audience](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/audience): The audience is not a passive recipient of the show. They are a co-creator of the shared reality — the third player in every scene.
- [Base Reality](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/base-reality): Base Reality is the normal, grounded, believable world that two characters inhabit at the top of a scene — before anything unusual happens.
- [Coherence](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/coherence): Coherence is the state in which all participants are tracking the same shared reality without having to explicitly negotiate it.
- [Environment](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/environment): Environment is the imagined physical and temporal conditions of the scene — the room, the weather, the objects.
- [Presence](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/presence): Presence is the capacity to sustain sensory contact with what is happening right now — with your partner, the environment, and yourself.
- [Warm-Up](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/warm-up): Warm-Up is the ritual that prepares performers for improvisation — not just physical warm-up but a neurological, ensemble.
- [Justification](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/justification): Justification is the act of finding or creating a reason why something that happened should have happened, within the reality of the scene.
- [Scene Structure](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/scene-structure): The arc of an improv scene — not a rigid template but a recognizable shape that emerges when the principles are working. Who are these people?
- [Bandwidth](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/bandwidth): Bandwidth is the total processing capacity available to participants in a shared interaction at any given moment.
- [Fear of Failure](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/fear-of-failure): Fear of Failure is the primary obstacle for every improv student — and the root cause of nearly every antipattern in the graph.
- [Point of View](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/point-of-view): Point of View is the filter through which a character sees everything — their specific, emotionally loaded lens on reality. UCB's core character concept.
- [Vulnerability](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/vulnerability): Vulnerability is the willingness to be seen without armor — to let your emotional state, your uncertainty.
- [Group Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/group-scene): Group Scene is a scene with three or more performers. Fundamentally different from two-person scenes.
- [Show Dynamic](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/show-dynamic): How a full improv show builds — not a set of scenes but a shaped experience with a beginning, middle, and end.
- [Beats (First / Second / Third)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/beats): The concept of first, second, and third beats in a Harold — how scenes recur and transform across the show.
- [Spontaneity](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/spontaneity): Acting on a first impulse before evaluating it. Johnstone's claim is that this is the default state, and that most adults were trained out of it.
- [Specificity](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/specificity): Specificity is naming the particular rather than the category. Not a dog but a whippet with a limp.
- [Tilt](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/tilt): Tilt is the moment the established normality breaks. Johnstone's term for the event that turns a situation into a story.
- [Two-Person Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/two-person-scene): Two-Person Scene is the fundamental unit of all improv. Virtually every longform structure — Harold, Armando, La Ronde, Deconstruction.
- [Want](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/want): Want is what the character desires from the other person in this scene. Want is the dramatic engine.
- [Game Types](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/game-types): A taxonomy of the different categories of games that can emerge in improv scenes.
- [Premise](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/vocabulary/premise): Premise is the situation a scene is in before anything unusual has happened to it. Two people in an elevator. A daughter visiting her father.

## Techniques (49)

- [Commitment](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/commitment): Commitment is the willingness to fully invest in a choice, even — especially — when you're unsure it's the "right" one.
- [Active Listening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/active-listening): Active listening in improv goes beyond hearing words. It means receiving everything your scene partner is communicating — their words, tone.
- [The Obvious Choice](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/obvious-choice): The obvious choice is the practice of acting on your first impulse without censoring it — before the internal editor intervenes with something "better."
- [Editing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/editing): Editing is how to end scenes. One of the hardest ensemble skills — it requires reading the scene from outside while respecting what's happening inside.
- [Emotional Truth](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/emotional-truth): Emotional truth is the quality of sending signals that match the character's actual internal state — without distortion, commentary, or ironic distance.
- [Accepting the Offer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/accepting-the-offer): Accepting the offer is the disciplined practice of receiving incoming information and treating it as valid before you evaluate it.
- [Space Work](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/space-work): Physically handling an environment that is not there — objects, distances, weight. The detail is what makes an invented room real to an audience.
- [Initiation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/initiation): Initiation is the craft of starting a scene — making one specific choice that implies the world, the relationship.
- [Yes, And: The First Rule of Improv](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/yes-and): Improv's best-known shorthand: accept what your partner established, then add to it. The yes is acceptance of the reality, not agreement with the character.
- [Suggestion](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/suggestion): Suggestion is how to take and use audience input. The suggestion is the ritual that proves the show is improvised, gives the audience ownership.
- [Do, Feel, Say](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/do-feel-say): Do, Feel, Say is a three-step ordering principle for authentic scene work: take a physical action first, let the emotion arrive from that action, then.
- [Let Yourself Be Changed](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/let-yourself-be-changed): The practice of allowing your partner's offers to visibly, behaviorally alter your character's state — rather than absorbing them without effect.
- [Physicality](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/physicality): Physicality is building character from the body first — not from concept, biography, or dialogue.
- [Safety in the Room](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/safety-in-the-room): Safety in the Room is creating the conditions under which vulnerability, risk, and honest play become possible.
- [Connections](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/connections): Finding thematic links across unrelated scenes in a Harold or longform show — the "it was all one thing" realization.
- [Reading the Room](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/reading-the-room): Reading the Room is the real-time perceptual skill of sensing the audience's collective state and adjusting performance choices accordingly.
- [Reincorporation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/reincorporation): Reincorporation is bringing back an element from earlier in the scene or show so that it returns with added significance, changed meaning.
- [Pacing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/pacing): Pacing is speed and rhythm management — within scenes and across shows. One of the skills that most separates experienced performers from intermediates.
- [Side-Coaching](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/side-coaching): Side-coaching is Viola Spolin's core teaching method: coaching players during the exercise, not stopping to lecture.
- [Support Moves](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/support-moves): Support Moves are what you do when you're NOT in the scene. Backline behavior is where ensemble is built or broken.
- [Audience Relationship](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/audience-relationship): The dynamic, bidirectional exchange between performers and audience in which both parties actively shape the performance.
- [If This, Then What?](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/if-this-then-what): If This, Then What? is the UCB engine for exploring game. Once the first unusual thing is identified, you don't simply repeat it — you ask.
- [Rest Beat](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/rest-beat): Rest Beat is the return to base reality between heightened beats of the game. Rest beats are what give each escalation its impact — without them.
- [Elevating](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/elevating): Elevating is the practice of taking your partner's offer and making it look intentional, important, and brilliant — even (especially) when it wasn't.
- [Endowment](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/endowment): Endowment is giving your scene partner qualities, attributes, or history through your behavior toward them.
- [Gratitude Reframing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/gratitude-reframing): Gratitude reframing is the practice of converting your internal response to unexpected input from evaluation to reception.
- [Failing Forward](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/failing-forward): Failing Forward is the skill of metabolizing on-stage failure — a dropped scene, a missed connection, a joke that dies — and converting it into material.
- [Giving Notes](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/giving-notes): Giving Notes is how to give feedback after scenes and shows — the teacher's and director's core skill.
- [Opening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/opening): Opening is the 3-5 minute ensemble ritual that transforms a single audience suggestion into multiple themes, ideas, and premises for a longform show.
- [Emotional Range](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/emotional-range): Emotional Range is accessing the full spectrum of emotion in scenes — not just the comfortable defaults.
- [Mapping](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/mapping): Mapping is a specific game type where one reality is played through the lens of another entirely.
- [Status Dynamics](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/status-dynamics): The mastery-level work on status is not "who is high and who is low" — it is the movement of status within a scene.
- [Straight Man](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/straight-man): Straight Man is the player who sees the world the way the audience does — the grounding force that makes the game player's unusual behavior legible.
- [Tag Run](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/tag-run): A rapid sequence of tag-outs exploring one game or pattern across multiple contexts.
- [Viewpoints](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/viewpoints): Viewpoints is a movement-based training system that splits physical awareness into nine named channels — tempo, duration, kinesthetic response.
- [Organic Opening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/organic-opening): Organic Opening is a group free-association opening that generates raw thematic material for a Harold or other longform show.
- [Pattern Break](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/pattern-break): Breaking an established pattern for effect. The audience has been trained to expect it, which is what makes the break land — and why timing decides it.
- [Playing Against Type](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/playing-against-type): Playing Against Type is subverting the audience's expectations at the character level. The tough guy who is tender. The librarian who is dangerous.
- [Stage Presence](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/stage-presence): Stage Presence is the ability to project your internal state outward so the audience can receive it.
- [Backline Craft](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/backline-craft): Backline Craft is what you do when you're NOT in the scene — standing at the back or sides of the stage, watching, tracking patterns.
- [Character Through Game](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/character-through-game): The UCB principle that character emerges from the game pattern, not from biography, backstory, or accent.
- [Curriculum Design](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/curriculum-design): Curriculum Design is how to sequence improv concepts for progressive skill-building — the meta-skill of designing a learning path from beginner to mastery.
- [Game Evolution](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/game-evolution): How a game transforms within a scene — not just repeating at higher intensity, but changing in kind. Four modes of evolution.
- [Meisner Technique](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/meisner-technique): Meisner Technique is an actor training method built on a single instruction: put your attention on the other person and respond to what they actually do.
- [Story Spine](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/story-spine): A fixed sequence of eight sentence stems that produces a complete story with a beginning, a turn, consequences and an ending.
- [Analogous Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/analogous-scene): Analogous Scene is a second or third beat scene that transplants the game from an earlier scene into a completely different context.
- [Heat and Weight](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/heat-and-weight): Heat and Weight is managing the two poles of energy in an improv show. Heat is high energy — fast pace, loud voices, big physicality, comic escalation.
- [Run](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/run): Run is a rapid-fire sequence of short scenes or callbacks that builds momentum toward a show's climax.
- [Sweep Edit](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/techniques/sweep-edit): The sweep edit is the Harold's signature transition device. One player walks briskly across the front of the stage.

## Exercises and games (27)

- [Gift Giving](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/gift-giving): Be Thankful — receiving unexpected input as a gift rather than a problem. Two players face each other.
- [Blind Offer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/blind-offer): The perceptual foundation of Be Supportive — reading your partner's physical offers and building a reality that serves them.
- [Mirroring](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/mirroring): Two players face each other and move in unison with no agreed leader, slowly enough that an observer cannot tell who is initiating.
- [One-Word Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/one-word-scene): Surrender and letting go of control — which produces simplicity as a byproduct. Also known as "One Word At A Time" or "One Word Story."
- [First Line Drill](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/first-line-drill): Each player steps out, commits to one declarative opening line, and stops. Trains starting a scene before you know where it goes.
- [One-Word Story](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/one-word-story): A circle tells one story, one word per person, and nobody is allowed to know where it is going. Stand in a circle.
- [Pass the Clap](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/pass-the-clap): Two people clap at the same instant, round a circle, until the group stops passing a clap and starts keeping one. Stand in a circle.
- [Status Transfer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/status-transfer): Play a scene in which the two characters have to swap high and low status by the end, without ever naming that it is happening.
- [Zip Zap Zop](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/zip-zap-zop): Stand in a circle and pass a clap with the words zip, zap and zop in strict order, with sharp eye contact and no hesitation.
- [Directed Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/directed-scene): Two players run a scene while a side-coach calls adjustments from offstage. The players fold each note in without stopping or acknowledging it.
- [Emotion Switch](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/emotion-switch): Play an ordinary scene. A caller names a new emotion at intervals, and both players shift to it completely and immediately while the story keeps going.
- [Fracture Repair Drill](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/fracture-repair-drill): Fracture recovery — the ability to re-establish shared reality when two players have diverged. Two players begin a scene.
- [Last Word Response](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/last-word-response): Two players hold a conversation in which every reply has to begin with the final word of what the other person just said.
- [Silent Space Work Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/space-work-scene): Space work — building and maintaining a shared physical environment with no dialogue. Two players. No speaking allowed. 2-3 minutes.
- [Yes, And Chain](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/yes-and-chain): Be Positive — the literal-words version of accepting and extending offers. A universal beginner drill taught at every school.
- [Big Booty](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/big-booty): Stand in a circle and number off, with one player as Big Booty. Keep a clap-and-slap rhythm going; on your beat call your own number then someone else's.
- [Bippity Bippity Bop](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/bippity-bippity-bop): Somebody stands in the middle, points at a player and says "bippity bippity bop." The player has to get "bop" out before the caller finishes the phrase.
- [Emotional Honesty Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/emotional-honesty-scene): Two players hold a scene in which every line has to say what the character actually feels. No deflecting, no joking it away.
- [No Backspace Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/no-backspace-scene): Irreversibility — the felt experience of path dependence. Borrows from Johnstone's New Choice mechanic but enforces forward rather than replacing.
- [Questions Only](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/questions-only): Two players hold a scene in which every line must be a question — and the exercise is most useful for what it reveals about the habit.
- [Sound Ball](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/sound-ball): A circle. You throw an imaginary ball to somebody and make a sound as it leaves your hands.
- [The Machine](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/the-machine): It needs no equipment and no preparation, which is the whole category party games is drawn from — the ones that need nothing at all travel furthest.
- [What Are You Doing?](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/what-are-you-doing): The standard first exposure to space work, and the reason most improvisers can mime at all. Two players, or a line taking turns in pairs.
- [Yes, Let's](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/yes-lets): Somebody says "let's paint the fence." Everybody answers "Yes, let's!" and starts painting the fence.
- [Genre Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/genre-scene): Play a scene in an assigned genre — noir, horror, nature documentary — committing to its conventions sincerely rather than sending them up.
- [Group Mind Cultivation](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/group-mind-cultivation): The group moves, counts or makes sound together with no leader and no discussion, restarting every time two people collide or hesitate.
- [Organic Opening Drill](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/exercises/organic-opening-exercise): Group free-association, thematic extraction, comfort with ambiguity, ensemble coherence.

## Formats (24)

- [The Harold: Improv's Most Important Long-Form Format](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/harold): The foundational longform improv structure. First performed by The Committee in California in 1967 and named, as a joke, on the drive home.
- [Theatresports](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/theatresports): Theatresports is Keith Johnstone's competitive improv format. Two teams perform improvised scenes head-to-head, judged by the audience.
- [Montage](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/montage): Montage is the most free-flowing longform format — a series of scenes with no required structure, no mandated group games.
- [Scenes from a Hat](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/scenes-from-a-hat): Audience suggestions are written on slips, drawn at random, and played as rapid scenes of ten to thirty seconds, cut the moment they land.
- [Genre Format](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/genre-format): Longform improv performed within the conventions of a specific genre — film noir, horror, Western, rom-com, musical.
- [Narrative Longform](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/narrative-longform): Narrative longform is longform improv that creates a coherent story with beginning, middle, and end — an improvised play or film.
- [Freeze Tag](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/freeze-tag): Freeze Tag is the most universal shortform improv game. Two performers begin a scene. At any point, someone on the sideline calls "Freeze!"
- [The Monoscene: One Scene, No Edits](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/monoscene): One scene, held for the whole set. Same location, same people, time moving roughly as it moves in life.
- [Gorilla Theatre](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/gorilla-theatre): Each performer takes a turn pitching a scene to the audience and then directing the others in it. The audience rewards the directors whose scenes work.
- [Micetro](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/micetro): Micetro is Keith Johnstone's elimination format (also spelled "Maestro"). Individual performers compete.
- [Organic Longform](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/organic-longform): No opening, no beat count and no set scene order — the ensemble starts a scene and lets the shape of the show come from what the material turns out to need.
- [Blind Line](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/blind-line): Before the show the audience writes lines on slips of paper, which are scattered face-down on the stage.
- [Bus Stop](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/bus-stop): One player is waiting at a bus stop and has a reason to stay there. Another arrives playing somebody specific.
- [Musical Improv: How Improvised Songs Get Made](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/musical-improv): Improvised scenes performed with live musical accompaniment, where performers spontaneously create songs — lyrics, melody, and sometimes choreography.
- [Party Quirks](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/party-quirks): Party Quirks is one of the most recognisable shortform games, and the one most often played badly. A host throws a party knowing nothing.
- [Story Story Die](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/story-story-die): A line of players tells a single story, and a conductor decides who is telling it.
- [Superheroes](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/superheroes): A hero is facing a crisis and calls for help. The player who enters is named by the one already there — Captain Mild Disappointment, The Human Tuesday.
- [The Alphabet Game](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/alphabet-game): Two players run a scene in which every line starts with the next letter of the alphabet.
- [The Deconstruction](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/deconstruction): A long form built by Del Close with The Family at ImprovOlympic, in which one unresolved scene becomes the material for everything that follows.
- [Two-Headed Expert](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/two-headed-expert): Two players stand together as one person — the world's leading authority on whatever the audience named — and answer questions one word at a time.
- [Two-Person Longform](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/two-person-longform): Two performers hold a full show of 25 to 60 minutes with no ensemble to edit for them, either as one continuous reality or as a story told with time jumps.
- [World's Worst](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/worlds-worst): World's Worst is a shortform game in which a category is announced — world's worst doctor, world's worst person to sit next to on a plane.
- [Armando](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/armando): Armando is a monologue-driven longform format where a monologist tells true personal stories that inspire improvised scenes.
- [La Ronde](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/practice/formats/la-ronde): La Ronde is a character-chain longform format where each two-person scene shares one character with the next.

## Lessons (25)

- [Building on Offers: The Engine of Scene Work](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/building-on-offers): Every improv scene is a chain of offers given and received. Understanding this chain - and what breaks it - is the first real skill an improviser develops.
- [Presence and Commitment: Being Fully in the Scene](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/presence-and-commitment): The two invisible skills that separate okay improv from electric improv are presence and commitment. Neither is a technique you perform - they're states you inhabit.
- [The Conversation That Felt Like Magic: What Was Happening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/conversation-that-felt-like-magic): Think about the last conversation where you lost track of time.
- [The Empty Stage Problem: Building Reality From Nothing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/empty-stage-problem): Imagine you're standing on a stage. Wooden floor, bright lights in your face. No props. No set. No script.
- [The First Rule You Already Know: Yes, And in Practice](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/first-rule-you-already-know): Let's watch a scene break.
- [The Hardest Thing You'll Never Plan: Actually Listening](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/hardest-thing-youll-never-plan): Accepting what your partner gives you is the first principle. But it assumes you actually heard what they gave you. And that turns out to be the harder problem.
- [Clear Signal, Simple Signal: How to Be Understood](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/clear-signal-simple-signal): So far we've talked about receiving — accepting offers, staying present, integrating surprises. Now we need to talk about sending. Because you're always transmitting, whether you intend to or not.
- [The Physics of Every Room: The Five Principles Applied](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/physics-of-every-room): Let's name what we've been building toward.
- [The System Underneath: Why Improv Works](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-system-underneath): Before you learn the moves, learn the physics.
- [Quieting the Planning Mind: Responding Without Rehearsing](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/quieting-the-planning-mind): You know the feeling. Your scene partner says something and instead of responding, your brain launches a search: What's the funny thing to say? What's the right move?
- [Diagnosing Scene Failure: A Vocabulary for What Went Wrong](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/diagnosing-scene-failure): You know the scene didn't work. You can feel it. But when someone asks "what happened?" all you can say is "I don't know, it just... died."
- [The Plateau Is a Map: Breaking Through the Intermediate Wall](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-plateau-is-a-map): Around the two-year mark — roughly Level 3 or 4 — every improviser tells themselves the same thing: I am terrible at improv.
- [The Game Beneath the Game: Advanced Pattern Mechanics](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-game-beneath-the-game): You know how to find the game. You can heighten it. You know when to rest. That's Level 3 work. Here's Level 5.
- [Character as Discovery: Beyond Accents and Attitudes](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/character-as-discovery): Most improv characters are built from the neck up — a voice, an attitude, maybe an occupation. Mastery-level character work starts from the body, the game, and the relationship.
- [Beyond the Harold: The Longform Landscape](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/beyond-the-harold): You've learned the Harold. You can run its beats, find its games, make its connections. Now what?
- [Show as Architecture: Building a Shaped Experience](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/show-as-architecture): A great improv show isn't a set of scenes. It's a shaped experience — with a beginning that establishes, a middle that develops, and an end that converges.
- [Playing Together at the Highest Level: Ensemble Craft](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/playing-together-at-the-highest-level): Every improv student learns "make your partner look good." At the mastery level, you stop thinking about it — your partner's success becomes indistinguishable from your own.
- [The Inner Game Expanded: Depth, Vulnerability, Transfer](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-inner-game-expanded): The outer game of improv is technique — yes-and, game, heightening, editing. The inner game is everything underneath: the emotional honesty, the willingness to be changed.
- [The Performer's Edge: Artistry Beyond Technique](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-performers-edge): At a certain point, you know the techniques. You can find the game, heighten it, edit well, support your teammates. The question shifts from "how do I do this?" to "who am I when I do this?"
- [The Teacher's Toolkit: From Performer to Pedagogue](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-teachers-toolkit): Performing well and teaching well are different skills. What the transition actually requires: safety first, then structure, then notes.
- [Traditions in Tension: Where the Schools Disagree](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/traditions-in-tension): There is no single "improv." There are at least five major traditions, each with distinct philosophies, and they disagree on fundamental questions.
- [On Shaping Shared Reality: Your Model of Their Model](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/shaping-shared-reality): You can't see into someone else's model of the world. You only have your model of their model — and it's almost always wrong. This is the first thing to get honest about.
- [The Anatomy of a Scene: Relationship, Want and Where](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/anatomy-of-a-scene): Before game, before format, before any of the advanced mechanics — there is the scene. Two people, a space, a relationship, and something at stake. Everything in improv is built from this unit.
- [The Connective Tissue: How Scenes Become Shows](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-connective-tissue): Callbacks, reincorporation and the other moves that link scenes to each other, and turn a run of unrelated pieces into one show.
- [The Practice Lab: Exercises for Every Level](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/threads/the-practice-lab): Every improv skill is trainable through exercises that make the right behavior structurally unavoidable.

## Learning paths (11)

- [Foundations: Your First Steps in Improv](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/beginner-foundations): A 7-day beginner program for learning the essential principles and first habits of improv.
- [The Physics of Connection](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/physics-of-connection): What improv reveals about every conversation you'll ever have. A guide to the invisible forces that make human connection work — and what breaks it.
- [Systems of Improv: A Thinking Person's Guide](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/systems-of-improv): Why improv works, explained as a system, for people who need the reasoning before the practice. Starts with the physics and ends with the exercises.
- [The Self-Coaching Toolkit](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/self-coaching-toolkit): A diagnostic vocabulary for improvisers who can feel what went wrong but cannot name it. Stop saying the scene just died and say what actually happened.
- [Advanced Game and Character](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/advanced-game-and-character): Beyond finding the game and making a choice. How games evolve, invert and break, and character built from body, status and game rather than accent.
- [Mastering the Form](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/mastering-the-form): You know Harold and you can do montage. Now what? Every major longform format, what each one demands, and how show craft shapes a run of scenes.
- [The Art of Ensemble](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/the-art-of-ensemble): Performing at the highest level: backline craft, ensemble coherence, managing performance state, and the practices that make group mind more than a metaphor.
- [Improv for Everyday Life](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/improv-for-life): The principles improvisers use on stage work everywhere — conversations, relationships, work, and the moments that matter. No stage required.
- [Improv for Teams and Leaders](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/improv-for-teams): What improv ensembles know about trust, collaboration, and group dynamics — applied to teams that need to work together without a script.
- [Teaching Improv: From Performer to Pedagogue](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/teaching-improv): For good improvisers asked to teach. Explaining why it works, structuring a class, giving feedback that changes behaviour, and making the room safe.
- [The Improv Reference Guide](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/paths/reference-guide): A cross-referenced analysis of improvisation across five traditions — Johnstone, Spolin, Close, UCB and Annoyance — with sources and counter-positions.

## Traditions

- [Keith Johnstone](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/traditions/johnstone): Status, spontaneity, and the Theatresports school.
- [Spolin and the Point of Concentration](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/traditions/spolin): Theater games, side-coaching, and the origin of the exercise.
- [iO and the Harold](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/traditions/close): Del Close, Charna Halpern, and long-form as art.
- [Upright Citizens Brigade](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/traditions/ucb): Game of the scene, base reality, and the UCB manual.
- [Annoyance Theatre / TJ & Dave](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/traditions/annoyance): Take care of yourself first, and the slow-play two-person show.

## Podcasts (3)

- [Deep Cuts Podcast](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/listen/deep-cuts): The ideas underneath improv, explored in depth. Full narrative conversations about game, character, ensemble, teaching, and the system.
- [The Improv Lab Podcast](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/listen/improv-lab): One concept. Six minutes. Try it tonight. Quick explainers for principles and exercises — the building blocks of the craft.
- [The Physics of Connection Podcast](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/listen/physics-of-connection): Improv's discoveries about human connection, applied to your actual life. No stage required. Chris has a problem; Sarah has a framework.

## Tools

- [Improv Exercise Picker](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker): Find an exercise by level and skill focus.
- [Improv Prompt Generator](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/improv-prompt-generator): Ranked scene starters for any room, on demand.
- [Beginner Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/beginner): Easy improv exercises for groups with no experience. Each one builds listening, presence, or collaboration — no performance skills required.
- [Beginner Presence & Listening Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/beginner/presence): Exercises that train sustained attention, active listening, and being fully in the moment.
- [Beginner Ensemble & Group Mind Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/beginner/ensemble): Exercises that build shared awareness, group coordination, and the ability to create as one.
- [Beginner Courage & Commitment Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/beginner/courage): Exercises that practice bold choices, full commitment, and acting before overthinking.
- [Beginner Physicality & Space Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/beginner/physicality): Exercises that develop body awareness, spatial work, and physical communication.
- [Intermediate Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/intermediate): Exercises for improvisers who know the basics and want to push past the plateau. Focus on emotional range, status, recovery, and scene-level skills.
- [Intermediate Courage & Commitment Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/intermediate/courage): Exercises that practice bold choices, full commitment, and acting before overthinking.
- [Intermediate Recovery & Adaptation Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/intermediate/recovery): Exercises that train handling mistakes, staying flexible, and building from the unexpected.
- [Advanced Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/advanced): Exercises for experienced performers working on ensemble depth, show craft, and artistic voice. Assumes comfort with game, character, and longform.
- [Advanced Ensemble & Group Mind Improv Exercises](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/tools/exercise-picker/advanced/ensemble): Exercises that build shared awareness, group coordination, and the ability to create as one.

## Reading list — the works this site cites (32)

- [Truth in Comedy — Halpern, Close, Johnson (1994)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/truth-in-comedy): The first book to write the Harold down, and the source of most of what Chicago longform believes about itself.
- [Impro — Keith Johnstone (1979)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/impro-johnstone): The book modern improv is downstream of. More of the vocabulary in use today starts here than in any other single source.
- [Improvisation for the Theater — Viola Spolin (1963)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/spolin-improvisation-for-theater): The foundational text of improvisational theatre pedagogy, and the origin of the phrase "theatre games".
- [UCB Comedy Improvisation Manual (2013)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/ucb-manual): The most systematic book ever written about improv. Where Truth in Comedy is a manifesto, this is a curriculum: definitions, worked examples.
- [Impro for Storytellers — Keith Johnstone (1999)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/impro-storytellers-johnstone): Johnstone's second book, written twenty years after Impro, and the inverse of it in almost every respect.
- [Improvise — Mick Napier (2004)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/napier-improvise): The book that argues the rules are the problem. Napier founded the Annoyance Theatre in Chicago.
- [Improv Nonsense Substack — Will Hines (ongoing)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/hines-substack): Will Hines, longtime UCB teacher, writing the most prolific contemporary blog on improv pedagogy — and arguing with UCB orthodoxy while he does it.
- [Improvisation at the Speed of Life — TJ & Dave (2015)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/tj-dave-speed-of-life): The method of the most celebrated two-person partnership in modern improv, set down in detail.
- [Behind the Scenes — Mick Napier (2015)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/napier-behind-the-scenes): Napier's second book is about the show rather than the scene: how a long form is assembled, when to cut, and what a director can say mid-run.
- [Improvise Freely — Patti Stiles (2021)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/stiles-improvise-freely): The strongest published improv source on consent and safety, arguing that safety is what makes risk affordable rather than what you trade against it.
- [How to Be the Greatest Improviser on Earth — Hines (2016)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/hines-greatest-improviser): A practitioner's guide organizing improv around behavioral mantras: Be Present, Be Changeable, Be Brave, Be Playful.
- [Improv Nerd Podcast & Blog — Jimmy Carrane (ongoing)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/carrane-improv-nerd): Chicago-based improviser, teacher, and host of one of the longest-running improv interview podcasts.
- [Sanford Meisner on Acting — Meisner & Longwell (1987)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/meisner-on-acting): A transcribed narrative of one acting class across fifteen months, in which the repetition exercise is taught rather than explained.
- [An Actor Prepares — Constantin Stanislavski (1936)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/stanislavski-actor-prepares): The system nearly every later acting method argues with, including the improv lineages that reject its inward turn.
- [Group Genius — Keith Sawyer (2007)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/sawyer-group-genius): The strongest academic bridge between improv practice and creativity research.
