- [The Viewpoints Book — Anne Bogart & Tina Landau (2005)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/viewpoints-bogart-landau): The standard written source for Viewpoints, and the reason the method spread beyond the handful of companies practising it.
- [Attention and Effort — Daniel Kahneman (1973)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/attention-and-effort-kahneman): The foundational capacity model of attention. Establishes that attention is a limited, general-purpose resource pool with flexible allocation.
- [Standing in Space — Mary Overlie (2016)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/overlie-standing-in-space): Overlie's own account of the Six Viewpoints, published four decades after she began teaching them and eleven years after the adaptation most people read.
- [Art by Committee — Charna Halpern (2006)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/halpern-art-by-committee): Halpern's follow-up to Truth in Comedy, and the place the Harold gets revised by the person who spent two decades watching it run.
- [Christopher Wickens — Multiple Resources (2002)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/wickens-multiple-resources): Why some things combine effortlessly and others cannot be done at once at all. The correction that keeps the bandwidth law from being too crude to use.
- [Daring Greatly — Brené Brown (2012)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/brown-daring-greatly): Vulnerability as a practice rather than a temperament, and courage as something accumulated by repetition inside a container safe enough to fail in.
- [Frame Analysis — Erving Goffman (1974)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/goffman-frame-analysis): Goffman's account of the frames people use to answer, silently and continuously, the question of what is going on here.
- [Improvised Dialogues — R. Keith Sawyer (2003)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/sawyer-improvised-dialogues): Sawyer analysed improvised performance as conversation data — the academic case that coherent structure emerges from interaction nobody planned.
- [Limb & Braun — Spontaneous Musical Performance (2008)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/limb-braun-jazz-improvisation): The most-cited piece of evidence that improvisation has a distinct neural signature.
- [Nelson Cowan — The Magical Number 4 (2001)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/cowan-magical-number-four): Where the number comes from. Everywhere this site says your working memory holds about four things, this is the source.
- [The Improv Handbook — Salinsky & Frances-White (2008)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/salinsky-improv-handbook): The most complete single-volume survey in the improv literature, and the one that takes the British and Australian lineage as seriously as Chicago.
- [Amy Edmondson — Psychological Safety in Work Teams (1999)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/edmondson-psychological-safety): The paper that gave psychological safety both its definition and its measure, and the anchor beneath what this site claims about groups.
- [Bossypants — Tina Fey (2011)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/fey-bossypants): The single most influential popularization of improv principles outside the improv world.
- [Cognitive Load During Problem Solving — John Sweller (1988)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/sweller-cognitive-load): The founding paper of cognitive load theory, and the reason this site says effort spent monitoring yourself is subtracted from the task itself.
- [Colin Cherry — The Cocktail Party Problem (1953)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/cherry-cocktail-party): The origin of the cocktail party problem, and the first evidence that attending to one voice is an act of exclusion rather than an act of focus.
- [Flow — Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1990)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/csikszentmihalyi-flow): The research behind the state improvisers describe as being in it: absorbed, unselfconscious, and no longer tracking your own performance.
- [Improv Wisdom — Patricia Ryan Madson (2005)](https://www.physicsofconnection.com/library/madson-improv-wisdom): Patricia Ryan Madson's treatment of improv principles as a way to live. Taught at Stanford for decades and read well beyond the theatre.

## Author

Jay Christopher — improv practitioner, teacher, and researcher. https://www.physicsofconnection.com/about
